experiment with nonempty $\Theta$. Let $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$ be a
pivot with common law $\nu$, and let $B\in\mathcal S$. Define
$$C(x):=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_\theta(x)\in B\}$$

least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.

the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by

derivations.claim: The full power set $2^{\mathbb Z}$ is an algebra of subsets closed under countable unions, so it is a sigma-algebra by [F5]. Explicitly set $P_\theta(A)=\frac13(\mathbf1_A(\theta-1)+\mathbf1_A(\theta)+\mathbf1_A(\theta+1))$ for every $A\subseteq\mathbb Z$. These values are nonnegative and have total mass $1$. For a pairwise disjoint sequence $A_m$, $\sum_mP_\theta(A_m)=\frac13\sum_{z\in\{-1,0,1\}}\sum_m\mathbf1_{A_m}(\theta+z) =\frac13\sum_{z\in\{-1,0,1\}}\mathbf1_{\cup_mA_m}(\theta+z) =P_\theta(\cup_mA_m)$. Thus it is countably additive, hence a probability measure, and specifies the experiment family in [F6]. Under $P_\theta$, $Q(X;\theta)$ assigns mass $1/3$ to each of $-1,0,1$, independently of $\theta$; hence $Q$ is a pivot with $P_\theta(Q\in B)=1$.

Define $F_Q(t):=P_\theta(Q\le t)$ and the generalized quantile $q_r:=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:F_Q(t)\ge r\}$. By the definition of $C$, the event $\{\theta\in C(X)\}$ is $\{|X-\theta|\le1\}$, which occurs for all three possible observations. Thus its probability and coverage equal $1$; this exceeds $4/5$, while [F4] also applies since $P_\theta(Q\in B)=1\ge4/5$. The pivot cdf is $0$ below $-1$, $1/3$ on $[-1,0)$, $2/3$ on $[0,1)$, and $1$ from $1$ onward. Thus the generalized $1/10$ and $9/10$ quantiles are $-1$ and $1$, and their closed interval contains all atoms.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$. Let $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$ be a
pivot with common law $\nu$, and let $B\in\mathcal S$. Define
$$C(x):=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_\theta(x)\in B\}$$
If $\nu(B)\ge1-\alpha$, then $C$ is a confidence set with coverage at
least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly
$1-\alpha$ for every parameter value. For an interval $B=[a,b]$ in
$\mathbb R$, exactness requires calibration of the actual probability
$\nu([a,b])$; quantile labels alone do not remove endpoint atoms.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: Let $G$ have the standard normal law. Its density is $\phi(u)=e^{-u^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, positive everywhere and bounded above by $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$, with total mass one by [F1]. Thus $\Phi(t)=P(G\le t)$ satisfies $0<\Phi(b)-\Phi(a)=\int_a^b\phi(u)\,du\le(b-a)/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for every $a<b$, proving strict increase and continuity. The events $\{G\le m\}$ and $\{G>-m\}$ increase to the whole space as integer $m\to\infty$; [F6] gives $\Phi(m)\to1$ and $P(G>-m)\to1$, hence $\Phi(-m)\to0$. Choose finite endpoints bracketing $1-\alpha/2$; [F5] gives a quantile between them, and strict increase gives uniqueness.
The standard normal density is symmetric and has no atoms. Therefore $\Phi(-z_{1-\alpha/2})=\alpha/2$, and the probability of $[-z_{1-\alpha/2},z_{1-\alpha/2}]$ is $1-\alpha$.

For every candidate mean $\eta$, $q_\eta(y)=(y-\eta)/\sigma$ is measurable and has standard normal law under $P_\eta$, so it is a pivot. The event $\eta\in[y-z\sigma,y+z\sigma]$ is exactly $-z\le q_\eta(y)\le z$; applying [F4] and [F3] gives exact coverage $1-\alpha$ for every $\eta$.

finite_checks.claim: The standard normal quantiles satisfy Phi(-z)=alpha/2 and Phi(z)=1-alpha/2.
finite_checks.result: Symmetry and zero endpoint masses give central acceptance probability 1-alpha.

risk_review.notes: Read all three steps and all seven suppliers. AC is expressly inherited from the normal-law construction. Positive bounded normal density yields a continuous strictly increasing CDF; increasing-event continuity gives both tail limits, and IVT gives a unique finite quantile for 0<alpha<1. Symmetry and absence of atoms give central mass 1-alpha. With sigma>0 the measurable affine pivot inverts in both directions to the stated interval. Zero variance and alpha endpoints are excluded. Use the experiment with data space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$, parameter set $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, and sampling law $P_{\mu,\sigma^2}=N(\mu,\sigma^2)^{\otimes n}$. Let $n\ge2$, $\sigma>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be the independent coordinates of the observation. Define
$$\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad S^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2,\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$
The map $x\mapsto\bar x$ is a statistic. The sample mean $\bar X$ and residual sum $S^2$ are independent,
$$\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-1}^2,\qquad S>0\ \text{almost surely},\qquad \widetilde T:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-1}.$$
For every $0<\alpha<1$, the interval
$$\left[\bar X-q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)\frac{S}{\sqrt n},\ \bar X+q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)\frac{S}{\sqrt n}\right]$$
has exact coverage $1-\alpha$, where $q_{n-1}(u)$ is the unique $u$-quantile of $t_{n-1}$ established in [[lem-student-t-and-f-cdfs-are-continuous-and-strictly-increasing]].

least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly
$1-\alpha$ for every parameter value. For an interval $B=[a,b]$ in
$\mathbb R$, exactness requires calibration of the actual probability
$\nu([a,b])$; quantile labels alone do not remove endpoint atoms.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra

Put $c=t_{
u,1-\alpha/2}$, which exists uniquely by [F2]. Symmetry and continuity give $F_{t_
u}(0)=1/2$; strict increase and $1-\alpha/2>1/2$ imply $c>0$. Since $F_{t_
u}(c)=1-\alpha/2$, symmetry gives $F_{t_
u}(-c)=\alpha/2$; continuity means neither endpoint is an atom, so $P(-c\le T_
u\le c)=1-\alpha$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a real-valued statistic whose sampling
distribution is parameter-free. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$. Let $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$ be a
pivot with common law $\nu$, and let $B\in\mathcal S$. Define
$$C(x):=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_\theta(x)\in B\}$$
If $\nu(B)\ge1-\alpha$, then $C$ is a confidence set with coverage at
least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly
$1-\alpha$ for every parameter value. For an interval $B=[a,b]$ in
$\mathbb R$, exactness requires calibration of the actual probability
$\nu([a,b])$; quantile labels alone do not remove endpoint atoms.

measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

derivations.claim: The sample sigma-algebra is the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^n$ by [F7]. The maximum map $m(x)=\max_i x_i$ satisfies $|m(x)-m(y)|\le\max_i|x_i-y_i|$, so it is continuous. The preimages of open sets are therefore open; since the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by open sets, preimages of every Borel set are Borel and $M=m(X)$ is measurable. Also $m/\theta$ is continuous because $\theta>0$. The coordinate variables are independent by [F1], and [F2] gives their product joint law.

If $0\le u\le1$, then $P_\theta(M/\theta\le u)=P_\theta(X_1\le u\theta,\ldots,X_n\le u\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n u=u^n$. For $u<0$ the probability is $0$, and for $u\ge1$ it is $1$. This law does not depend on $\theta$, so $M/\theta$ is a pivot by [F3].
The distribution function $u^n$ established in step 1.2 is continuous. Therefore $P_\theta(\alpha^{1/n}\le M/\theta\le1)=1-(\alpha^{1/n})^n=1-\alpha$. By [F5], pivot inversion gives exact coverage.

Since $\theta>0$, the inequality $\alpha^{1/n}\le M/\theta\le1$ is equivalent to $M\le\theta\le M/\alpha^{1/n}$. Thus the inverted set is $[M,M/\alpha^{1/n}]\cap(0,\infty)$, and [F4] identifies its coverage with the probability computed in step 2.1.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For all $x,y\in R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$ (x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkx^ky^{n-k}.$$

The natural-number coefficients act by repeated addition. The formula includes $n=0$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal Y,\mathcal G),(Q_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$, and let $0\le\alpha\le1$. For each
$\eta\in\Theta$, let $A_\eta\in\mathcal G$ be the acceptance event of a
test of the point null $\theta=\eta$, on the full observation space,
including any auxiliary randomization. Suppose
$Q_\eta(A_\eta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every $\eta\in\Theta$.
Then $C(y):=\{\eta\in\Theta:y\in A_\eta\}$
is a confidence set with coverage at least $1-\alpha$.

The probability bound is the point-null level condition written in terms of
acceptance events. For a randomized test, a rejection-probability function on
the original data space is not itself an acceptance event; the auxiliary
randomization must be part of the observation before applying this statement.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words
*nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of
[[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion.

1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nondecreasing on $I$.
2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on
   $I$.
3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nonincreasing on $I$.
4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on
   $I$.

Conversely, with no continuity hypothesis and no hypothesis at any other point:

5. If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing on $I$ and differentiable at a
   point $c \in I$ that is a limit point of $I$, then $f'(c) \ge 0$; if $f$ is
   nonincreasing and differentiable at such a $c$, then $f'(c) \le 0$.

**No strict converse is claimed here, and none is true.** Claim 5 gives the
weak inequality only, and it cannot be improved: an increasing function may have
a vanishing derivative at a point. That failure is recorded separately, as a
false statement later on this page, with its witness worked out on the companion
page. Reading claim 2 backwards is the single most common misuse of this
theorem, and this statement does not license it.

**Claims 1 to 4 need the interval; claim 5 does not.** The forward direction
runs through the mean value theorem on a segment joining two points of $I$, so
order-convexity is essential. Claim 5 is a statement about one point and uses
only that the difference quotients have a constant sign.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: The full power set of $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ is an algebra closed under countable unions, hence a sigma-algebra by [F5]. The binomial theorem [F1] gives $\sum_{j=0}^n\binom njp^j(1-p)^{n-j}=(p+1-p)^n=1$; all terms are nonnegative for $p\in[0,1]$, so [F6] makes the displayed masses a probability measure, including $p=0,1$. These laws form an experiment as in [F7].

For $k<n$, count pairs consisting of a $j$-element subset of an $n$-element set and a distinguished element inside it. Counting in the two orders gives $j\binom nj=n\binom{n-1}{j-1}$ for $1\le j\le k$. Counting instead a distinguished element outside the subset gives $(n-j)\binom nj=n\binom{n-1}j$ for $0\le j\le k$, by [F4]. The first identity is not used at $j=0$: in differentiating $p^j$, that boundary term is zero, so the first derivative sum starts at $j=1$, while the second identity includes $j=0$. Since $F_p(k)$ is a polynomial, it is continuous on $[0,1]$, and for $0<p<1$ termwise differentiation and the two identities give $$\frac{d}{dp}F_p(k) =\sum_{j=1}^k j\binom njp^{j-1}(1-p)^{n-j} -\sum_{j=0}^k(n-j)\binom njp^j(1-p)^{n-j-1} =-n\binom{n-1}k p^k(1-p)^{n-k-1}<0.$$ When $k=0$, the first sum is empty and the $j=0$ term of the second sum gives the same formula. By [F9], $F_p(k)$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$. Also $F_0(k)=1$ and $F_1(k)=0$ because $k<n$. Applying [F10] to this continuous polynomial on $[0,1]$ gives a point $U_k\in(0,1)$ with $F_{U_k}(k)=\alpha$; strict decrease makes it unique.

For each fixed candidate $p_0$, $F_{p_0}(k)$ is nondecreasing in integer $k$. Let $k_0$ be the least $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with $F_{p_0}(k)\ge\alpha$, which exists because $F_{p_0}(n)=1$. The deterministic test function is $\varphi_{p_0}(x)=\mathbf1_{\{F_{p_0}(x)<\alpha\}}$; it is measurable on this finite space. Its rejection event is $\{X<k_0\}$, whose probability is $0$ if $k_0=0$, and otherwise is $F_{p_0}(k_0-1)<\alpha$. The null is $\{p_0\}$, and the alternative $[0,1]\setminus\{p_0\}$ is nonempty; by [F8] the test size equals this rejection probability and is at most $\alpha$.

For an observed $x<n$, strict decrease of $F_p(x)$ in $p$ makes $\{p_0:F_{p_0}(x)\ge\alpha\}=[0,U_x]$; for $x=n$, the set is $[0,1]=[0,U_n]$. Thus $C(X)$ is precisely the inversion of those acceptance events. The level calculation in step 2.1 and [F3] imply its coverage is at least $1-\alpha$, in the sense of [F2].
